leaks.title: A 5-trade losing streak with no circuit breaker
leaks.evidence: The run cost −₹41,166 before it ended on its own.
leaks.fix: Cap the day at ₹16,941 of loss. Hitting it means the market isn't paying today and the terminal gets closed.

leaks.title: Short-term trades quietly becoming investments
leaks.evidence: 5 positions carried beyond the day, 0% profitable, −₹10,221 net.
leaks.fix: Name the holding period at entry and write it down. A trade that becomes a long-term hold after it moves against you is just an unexecuted stop.

leaks.title: Overtrading on busy days
leaks.evidence: Days with 4–6 trades account for −₹10,201 across 10 trades at 40% wins.
leaks.fix: Give yourself a hard count of three trades a day. Scarcity forces you to wait for the setup instead of inventing one.

traits.name: Moving the goalposts
traits.now: 9 positions lost more than half their value before being closed.
traits.why: A stop that exists only in your head is easy to move. Each time price reaches it, a new reason appears for giving the trade more room, and the planned small loss becomes a large one.
traits.ideal: Stops are placed with the broker at entry, so moving them requires a deliberate, visible action.

traits.name: Tilt
traits.now: Your longest losing run was 5 trades in a row, costing ₹41,166.
traits.why: After several losses, frustration takes over decision-making. Each new loss lowers the bar for the next entry, until trading becomes a way to vent rather than a process.
traits.ideal: A daily loss limit and a maximum number of consecutive losses, after which trading stops for the day.

traits.name: Chasing the same name
traits.now: 5 times you re-entered the same name on the same day you lost on it, losing ₹20,798 more.
traits.why: Losing on a specific stock or contract makes it personal. Re-entering is an attempt to win back from that particular instrument, as if it owed you something.
traits.ideal: After a loss on a name, that name is off-limits for the rest of the day.

traits.name: Short-term thinking in long trades
traits.now: Positions you carried for days lost ₹10,221, while your quick trades did better.
traits.why: A trade that was meant to be quick becomes a "long-term investment" once it goes red. The story changes to justify not closing it.
traits.ideal: The holding period is set at entry. A short-term trade that fails is closed, not reclassified.

traits.name: Recency bias
traits.now: Your win rate fell from 58% in your earlier trades to 39% in the later ones.
traits.why: Recent wins make the current approach feel right, so it is pushed harder even as conditions change. What worked last month gets applied to a market that has moved on.
traits.ideal: Setups are reviewed against recent market conditions, not just recent results.

traits.name: Rule erosion
traits.now: Your later trades won less often (39%) than your earlier ones (58%).
traits.why: Rules are easiest to follow at the start. Each small exception that works out makes the next one easier, until the rules are mostly gone.
traits.ideal: Rules are written, checked before each trade, and reviewed weekly.

traits.name: Self-attribution after streaks
traits.now: You had a 5-trade winning streak and a 5-trade losing streak.
traits.why: Winning streaks feel like skill and losing streaks feel like bad luck. Both are often the same process meeting different market conditions.
traits.ideal: Size and rules stay the same through streaks of either kind.

more.name: Overtrading
more.now: On days with 4 or more trades you lost ₹10,201 across 10 trades.
more.why: Busy days feel productive. But the more trades in a day, the lower the quality of each one, because the best setups don't appear on demand.
more.ideal: A daily trade limit. Fewer, better trades beat many average ones.

more.name: Boredom trades
more.now: Days with a single trade made ₹75,972; busy days lost ₹10,201.
more.why: Your first trade of the day is usually your best one, chosen with patience. Extra trades come from restlessness, not opportunity.
more.ideal: After the planned trade, the platform closes unless a pre-defined second setup appears.

more.name: Late-session fatigue
more.now: Your late-session trades return much less on average than your early ones.
more.why: Decision quality drops as the session goes on. Attention fades and the bar for a good setup quietly lowers.
more.ideal: The most important decisions are made when you are freshest; late trading is limited or stopped.

more.name: Calendar fixation
more.now: Your best weekday (Monday) and worst (Thursday) differ by ₹96,867.
more.why: Large differences between days point to routine and mindset rather than market structure. Your best day shows how you trade when conditions suit you.
more.ideal: Recreate the conditions of your best day (preparation, timing, mood) on the others.

net.ideal: Net P&L after costs is the only number that pays. Judge every change to your trading by its effect here.

gross.ideal: Gross P&L should comfortably exceed costs; if it barely does, trade less, not more.

costs.now: Costs were 0% of what your winners made.
costs.ideal: Costs under 15–20% of gross profit. Fewer trades with larger targets get you there.

winrate.ideal: Win rate only matters alongside payoff. 40% with 2:1 winners beats 60% with 1:2.

payoff.now: Average win is 2.07× the average loss.
payoff.ideal: A payoff above 1.5 gives room for a normal win rate to be profitable.

avgwin.ideal: Winners run to a planned target instead of being taken at the first sign of profit.

avgloss.ideal: Losers closed at a pre-set stop, so the average loss is smaller than the average win.

pf.ideal: A profit factor above 1.3 after costs is a sustainable edge.

worst.now: Your worst trade was ₹15,917, about 1.9 average wins.
worst.ideal: The worst trade is no bigger than one or two average wins.

costsPanel.ideal: Every trade expected to make several times its cost.

leaks.now: Losses are spread across many trades.
leaks.ideal: Leaks are fixed one at a time, starting with the most expensive.

curve.now: At the worst point you were ₹68,856 below your peak.
curve.ideal: A steady upward slope with shallow dips; deep drops mean risk per trade is too high.

instrument.ideal: Capital goes to the instrument where your results are best, not where the action is.

year.ideal: Improvement shows as each year being better than the last.

afterwinloss.now: After a loss your next trade averages ₹76; after a win, ₹3,938.
afterwinloss.ideal: The trade after a loss looks like any other trade: same size, same checklist.

diagnosis.ideal: A positive average trade after costs, held steady over hundreds of trades.

rules.now: Rules built from your own mistakes.
rules.ideal: Rules are followed before every trade, not just read once.

patterns.ideal: Do more of what works, pause what consistently doesn't.

psych.ideal: Awareness first; then one rule per habit, tested for a month.

premium.now: Results by the premium you paid.
premium.ideal: Pick strikes for probability and liquidity, not price.

expiryType.now: 60% of your options were weekly contracts.
expiryType.ideal: Match the expiry to how long your idea needs.

hold.ideal: Winners held at least as long as losers.

month.ideal: Most months profitable, with small losing months.

size.ideal: Size follows a formula, not conviction.

style.ideal: Holding period decided at entry, never changed because a trade is losing.

worstU.ideal: Repeat losers go on a pause list.
